description: We're Attack on Anthropic, six high school students from Canada who've spent an unreasonable amount of time in basements building robots, debugging code, and convincing ourselves that one more hour will fix everything. Between robotics competitions, hackathons, and questionable sleep schedules, we've developed a habit of turning simple ideas into engineering problems. We've spent enough time trying to make robots survive on Earth. Now we're curious about what's beyond the walls.
summary:
A spacecraft can look perfect on paper and still fail when something unexpected happens. We built MARGIN: ZERO to let people experience that challenge for themselves.

MARGIN: ZERO is an interactive spacecraft engineering game where players design an Earth-observation satellite, balancing choices like battery capacity, solar power, communications, and cost. They then put their design through a 16-hour simulated mission. But unlike most games, failure isn't the end. It's where the real challenge begins.

Players investigate what went wrong using recorded flight data, test which events actually caused the failure, and change one engineering decision before flying the exact same mission again. They can then test their design against 49 different simulated conditions to see how well it holds up.

Using hardware specifications catalogued in NASA publications alongside clearly identified assumptions, our goal is to make spacecraft engineering more accessible and engaging. Rather than simply teaching people how to build something that works, we want them to understand why it works, why it fails, and how to make it better.
details:
The Idea Behind MARGIN: ZERO

A spacecraft can meet every requirement on paper and still fail when something unexpected happens. A damaged solar array, a missed communication window, or a sudden increase in power consumption can be enough to end a mission.

But a failed mission raises a more interesting question: What actually went wrong, and could a different engineering decision have prevented it?

That's the question we built MARGIN: ZERO around.

MARGIN: ZERO is an interactive spacecraft engineering game where players design an Earth-observation satellite, fly it through a simulated mission, and investigate what happens when their design is pushed beyond its limits.

We didn't want players to simply receive a success or failure message and start over. We wanted them to understand their spacecraft well enough to explain what happened, identify the decisions that mattered, and test whether a different design would have survived.

In MARGIN: ZERO, failure isn't the end of the game. It's the beginning of the investigation.

How the Game Works

Players are responsible for designing MZ-01, a small Earth-observation satellite. They choose its scientific instrument, solar array, battery, communications system, orbit, and launch option while working within mass and budget limits.

Every choice comes with a trade-off. A larger battery can keep the spacecraft operating longer, but it adds weight and cost. A more capable instrument collects more data, but demands more power. Improving one part of the spacecraft doesn't necessarily improve the mission as a whole.

To make these decisions easier to understand, we built an interactive spacecraft blueprint and Systems Lab. As players change components, the spacecraft visualization responds. They can examine individual subsystems and see how solar generation, battery charging, power consumption, and communication opportunities change throughout an orbit.

Once they're satisfied with their design, they launch a 16-hour simulated mission.

For the default spacecraft, things don't go according to plan. Three scheduled anomalies affect its solar power, communications, and imaging workload. The spacecraft eventually loses power at T+11.4 hours, before completing its mission.

That failure opens the next stage: the Black Box.

Instead of immediately explaining the answer, the game presents players with the evidence. They can replay recorded telemetry, inspect affected subsystems, examine the sequence of events, and investigate possible causes.

One of the features we focused on most is the ability to test those causes. The game reruns the same mission with individual anomalies removed, allowing players to see whether the spacecraft would still have failed without each event. For the default design, both the solar-array fault and the increased imaging workload prove necessary to the power failure.

This makes the investigation more than a guessing game. Players aren't just identifying what happened before the failure. They're testing what actually made the difference.

With that evidence, they move to the What-If Replay.

Here, players change a single engineering decision and fly the mission again under identical conditions. The anomalies still occur at the same times, and every other part of the experiment remains unchanged.

For example, increasing the battery capacity from 180 Wh to 300 Wh allows the default spacecraft to complete all 16 hours. Players can compare the original and revised flights directly, including battery levels, mission duration, and science data returned to Earth.

The final stage, the Resilience Lab, asks another question: Just because a design survives one mission, does that mean it's reliable?

Players can test their spacecraft against 49 hypothetical combinations of solar-array damage and ground-station outages. The default design survives 23 of those conditions. A search across 27 candidate configurations identifies a more robust design that survives all 49, although it requires additional mass and cost.

These results aren't predictions of a real spacecraft's probability of survival. They're controlled scenarios designed to make an important engineering trade-off visible: preparing for difficult conditions can improve resilience, but those improvements have a cost.

What Makes Our Approach Different

The feature that best represents our project is the connection between failure, evidence, and redesign.

The investigation isn't a fixed sequence of answers written for one spacecraft. The flight recorder, subsystem behaviour, causal tests, and comparisons all come from the same deterministic simulation. Change the design or the conditions, and the evidence changes too.

That consistency lets players conduct meaningful experiments. They can form a hypothesis, change one variable, compare the outcome, and decide what to try next.

We also made a deliberate effort to keep the engineering accessible. MARGIN: ZERO follows a six-stage guided experience, so players aren't confronted with every graph and calculation at once. Someone unfamiliar with spacecraft engineering can follow the mission from beginning to end, while more curious players can explore the underlying telemetry, technical explanations, and design trade-offs.

We wanted the experience to be engaging without turning engineering into guesswork. The visuals help explain what's happening, but the decisions and outcomes are grounded in the simulation itself.

Development, Scientific Accuracy, and Impact

We developed MARGIN: ZERO as a browser-based application using React, TypeScript, and Vite.

Its deterministic simulation models orbital sunlight and eclipse periods, solar power generation, spacecraft energy consumption, battery capacity, onboard data storage, and communication opportunities. We used Vitest to check the model's behaviour, with 110 automated tests passing in the final tested build.

For our scientific foundation, we used NASA's 2026 State-of-the-Art of Small Spacecraft Technology report and NASA's Earth Fact Sheet. The spacecraft hardware specifications are based on manufacturer data catalogued in NASA publications, while orbital quantities are calculated using published Earth constants.

We also distinguish between sourced values, derived calculations, and assumptions throughout the application. Costs, payload behaviour, and anomaly conditions are illustrative choices made for the educational experience.

That distinction is important to us. MARGIN: ZERO is not flight-qualified spacecraft software, and our simplified model cannot represent every factor involved in a real mission. It doesn't attempt to simulate everything from thermal behaviour to spacecraft attitude and a complete communications link budget. Instead, we focused on a smaller set of interconnected systems that players can understand, experiment with, and learn from.

We see MARGIN: ZERO being useful for students, educators, and anyone interested in space exploration, including people who have never studied aerospace engineering. Because it runs directly in a browser, it requires no specialized software or equipment.

More importantly, we want it to introduce a way of thinking that extends beyond spacecraft design.

Engineering isn't only about finding a solution that works. It's about understanding the limits of that solution, recognizing the trade-offs behind it, and knowing what evidence to look for when something fails.

A spacecraft surviving one simulation doesn't tell the whole story. Neither does a failed mission. What matters is understanding the difference between the two, and being able to explain why.

That's what we hope players take away from MARGIN: ZERO:

Not just how to build something that works, but how to investigate why it didn't - and use what they learn to build something better.
